questions.stem: What is the aim of this investigation into specific heat capacity?

options.text: to find the specific heat capacity of water or another material
options.explanation: The measurement of c from supplied energy and temperature rise is the target.

options.text: to observe a constant temperature during melting
options.explanation: That is the changes-of-state practical.

options.text: to measure the latent heat of vaporisation
options.explanation: No boiling occurs in this investigation.

options.text: to compare the densities of liquids
options.explanation: Density is a different topic entirely.

questions.stem: Which is the independent variable in this investigation?

options.text: the room temperature
options.explanation: Room conditions are background controls, not the manipulated input.

options.text: the energy supplied by the heater
options.explanation: Energy in is what the experimenter controls and changes.

options.text: the temperature rise of the material
options.explanation: The rise is measured, making it the dependent variable.

options.text: the mass of the material
options.explanation: Mass is held fixed — a control variable.

questions.stem: How is the energy supplied by the immersion heater calculated?

options.text: mass × temperature rise
options.explanation: That product has no energy meaning without the capacity.

options.text: current ÷ time
options.explanation: Charge per second is not energy.

options.text: voltage × current × heating time
options.explanation: E = VIt is the electrical energy delivered.

options.text: voltage × current
options.explanation: That is power; the heating time factor is missing.

questions.stem: Why is the mass of the liquid a control variable?

options.text: changing the mass would break the thermometer
options.explanation: The risk is unfair comparison, not equipment damage.

options.text: mass cannot be measured in a laboratory
options.explanation: A balance measures it easily.

options.text: mass is the dependent variable
options.explanation: Temperature rise is the dependent variable.

options.text: the temperature rise per joule depends on the mass, so it must be fixed for a fair test
options.explanation: ΔQ = mcΔT ties the response to the mass.

questions.stem: A student starts with water at 5 °C on a cold bench instead of near room temperature. Why does this threaten the accuracy?

options.text: the large temperature gap with the surroundings adds uncontrolled energy exchange
options.explanation: Cold water draws in heat from the room, corrupting the energy account.

options.text: the thermometer cannot read 5 °C
options.explanation: Ordinary lab thermometers read far below 5 °C.

options.text: the heater stops working below 10 °C
options.explanation: Immersion heaters work at any starting temperature.

options.text: water has no specific heat capacity at 5 °C
options.explanation: The capacity is defined at all temperatures within the liquid state.

questions.stem: State the independent and dependent variables of this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the energy supplied by the heater; the dependent variable is the resulting temperature rise of the material.

questions.stem: State the equation used to compute the electrical energy supplied to the heater.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy = voltage × current × time, E = V × I × t.

questions.stem: Explain why the starting temperature is controlled near room temperature in this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy account assumes all the heater's joules go into the sample. If the sample starts well below room temperature, the surroundings donate extra heat during the run; if well above, the sample leaks heat out. Starting near room temperature keeps that unmeasured exchange small, so c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT) stays honest.

questions.stem: A heater runs at 10 V and 2.0 A for 500 s. Calculate the energy supplied.
Which instrument measures the mass of the water before heating?

options.text: the thermometer
options.explanation: The thermometer reads temperature.

options.text: a balance
options.explanation: The known mass comes from the balance reading.

options.text: a measuring cylinder
options.explanation: A cylinder measures volume; converting to mass invites density error.

options.text: the ammeter
options.explanation: The ammeter reads current.

questions.stem: Why must the immersion heater be fully submerged?

options.text: so the meters read more accurately
options.explanation: Meter accuracy is independent of submersion.

options.text: so the thermometer fits alongside
options.explanation: Thermometer placement is a separate matter.

options.text: so all the electrical energy is delivered into the water
options.explanation: Exposed heater sections waste energy to air, corrupting ΔQ.

options.text: so the water cannot boil
options.explanation: Submersion has nothing to do with suppressing boiling.

questions.stem: When should the stopwatch be started?

options.text: five minutes after heating starts
options.explanation: A late start loses energy from the account.

options.text: after the first temperature reading
options.explanation: The first reading belongs to the timed sequence.

options.text: when the water starts warming
options.explanation: Warming begins almost immediately; the switch-on moment is the reference.

options.text: at the same moment the heater is switched on
options.explanation: The energy ledger and the clock must open together.

questions.stem: Why is the beaker lagged or insulated in this set-up?

options.text: to reduce energy lost to the surroundings, a systematic error
options.explanation: Insulation keeps the measured ΔQ closer to the energy the water actually received.

options.text: to stop the water from changing state
options.explanation: The water is not meant to change state anyway at these temperatures.

options.text: to make the heater more powerful
options.explanation: Insulation does not change the heater's power.

options.text: to hold the thermometer upright
options.explanation: A stand does that job.

questions.stem: A student reads the voltmeter only at the end of the run. Why is this poor practice?

options.text: the voltmeter must be read by two students
options.explanation: Crew size is irrelevant to drift.

options.text: the supply can drift during the run, so the energy account needs readings throughout
options.explanation: E = VIt assumes steady V and I; only monitoring proves it.

options.text: voltmeters drain their batteries if read twice
options.explanation: Reading a voltmeter does not drain anything.

options.text: the final voltage is always wrong
options.explanation: A single reading is not always wrong; it is just unverified.

questions.stem: State the full equipment list for measuring the specific heat capacity of water.
questions.modelAnswer: A balance, insulated beaker, immersion heater, voltmeter, ammeter, stopwatch and thermometer.

questions.stem: State what should be measured before the heater is switched on.
questions.modelAnswer: The mass of the water on the balance, plus the initial temperature of the water and the meter readings.

questions.stem: Explain why the voltmeter and ammeter are read during the run and not only at the end.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy ledger uses E = VIt, which multiplies an average voltage and current by the time. If the supply sags or surges partway through, end-point readings misrepresent the energy actually delivered. Periodic meter readings verify that V and I stayed steady, or allow an averaged product to be used, keeping ΔQ honest.

questions.stem: A run delivers 10 000 J to 1.0 kg of water and the temperature climbs from 14 °C to 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity this suggests.
questions.modelAnswer: ΔT = 30 − 14 = 16 °C, so c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT) = 10 000 ÷ (1.0 × 16) = 625 J/kg °C — far below water's 4200, pointing to energy lost or misdelivered in the set-up.

questions.stem: Which columns belong in the results table?

options.text: only the final temperature
options.explanation: A single reading cannot support the analysis.

options.text: the student's names per interval
options.explanation: Roles may be noted elsewhere, not in the data table.

options.text: time, temperature, and meter readings for voltage and current
options.explanation: Together they let energy be computed against each temperature.

options.text: colour and smell of the water
options.explanation: Qualitative observations are not part of this quantitative ledger.

questions.stem: How is the cumulative energy at each interval obtained?

options.text: adding all the temperature readings so far
options.explanation: Temperatures are not additive into energy.

options.text: multiplying the mass by the elapsed time
options.explanation: Mass times time has no energy meaning.

options.text: reading it from the thermometer
options.explanation: The thermometer reads temperature, not energy.

options.text: voltage × current × the elapsed heating time
options.explanation: E = VIt with the running clock gives the accumulated energy.

questions.stem: Why pair each temperature with the energy delivered up to that moment?

options.text: the paired points let energy be plotted against temperature rise for a gradient method
options.explanation: Paired data is what the ΔQ–ΔT plot needs.

options.text: pairing makes the table look fuller
options.explanation: Presentation is not the purpose.

options.text: pairing is required by the exam board's form
options.explanation: The pairing serves the physics, not paperwork.

options.text: unpaired readings are invalid units
options.explanation: The readings are valid; pairing is for the analysis.

questions.stem: In the results-table image for this practical, what does the caption note about energy supplied?

options.text: energy supplied is constant whatever the meters say
options.explanation: The meters define the energy.

options.text: energy supplied equals voltage × current × time
options.explanation: The caption restates the E = VIt ledger law.

options.text: energy supplied equals mass × temperature rise
options.explanation: That is missing the capacity and the wrong ledger entirely.

options.text: energy supplied is read from the thermometer
options.explanation: Thermometers never read energy.

questions.stem: A table shows energy climbing in equal steps while the temperature rise per step shrinks. What does that suggest?

options.text: the thermometer is broken
options.explanation: A systematic flattening points to leakage, not breakage.

options.text: the meters are adding wrongly
options.explanation: Equal energy steps are exactly what steady meters show.

options.text: energy is leaking from the system faster as the water gets hotter
options.explanation: Hotter water loses more to the surroundings, so less of each step warms it.

options.text: the water's specific heat capacity is falling during the run
options.explanation: The capacity is effectively constant; leakage explains the curve.

questions.stem: State what each row of the results table represents.
questions.modelAnswer: Each row is one timed interval: the clock time, the temperature read then, and the meter readings that fix the energy delivered by then.

questions.stem: State the relationship the completed table is designed to reveal.
questions.modelAnswer: It shows the proportionality between the energy supplied and the temperature rise, whose ratio through the mass gives the specific heat capacity.

questions.stem: Explain why a cumulative energy column is more useful than recording energy only at the end of the run.
questions.modelAnswer: A cumulative column turns the run into many paired (energy, temperature) points, so the analysis can use the gradient of the whole dataset instead of trusting one end-point division. It also exposes any non-linearity — drift, leakage, boiling — that a single final figure would silently hide.

questions.stem: A heater delivers 10 000 J in total and the table's final temperature rise is 16 °C for a 1.0 kg sample. Using c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT), calculate the capacity the table suggests and compare it to water's 4200 J/kg °C.
questions.modelAnswer: c = 10 000 ÷ (1.0 × 16) = 625 J/kg °C. That is far below 4200 J/kg °C, so only a fraction of the heater's energy actually warmed the sample — losses dominated the ledger.

questions.stem: What is plotted on each axis for the gradient analysis?

options.text: energy vertically, temperature rise horizontally
options.explanation: That inversion makes the gradient mc instead — workable but not the of-record layout.

options.text: time on both axes
options.explanation: Time is the sampling rhythm, not an analysis axis here.

options.text: mass vertically, voltage horizontally
options.explanation: Mass is fixed; voltage is an intermediate reading.

options.text: temperature rise vertically, energy supplied horizontally
options.explanation: That orientation gives gradient = ΔT/ΔQ = 1/(mc).

questions.stem: What does the gradient of the ΔT–ΔQ line equal?

options.explanation: From ΔT = (1/mc)·ΔQ with mass fixed.

options.text: m × c
options.explanation: That is the reciprocal layout's gradient.

options.text: c on its own
options.explanation: The mass factor must be divided out.

options.text: ΔQ × ΔT
options.explanation: Gradients are ratios of changes, not products.

questions.stem: How does heat lost to the surroundings bias the measured specific heat capacity?

options.text: it makes the value random rather than biased
options.explanation: Leakage is repeatable and one-directional — systematic.

options.text: it makes the measured value too high, because ΔQ is overcounted for the rise achieved
options.explanation: c = ΔQ/(mΔT) grows when ΔQ includes joules that never warmed the sample.

options.text: it makes the measured value too low
options.explanation: Missing energy from the sample's side, not excess, would lower it.

options.text: it has no effect because the meters are accurate
options.explanation: The meters are accurate about energy delivered — including the wasted part.

questions.stem: Which improvement most directly reduces the dominant systematic error?

options.text: using a shorter stopwatch
options.explanation: Timing precision is not the systematic driver.

options.text: writing neater tables
options.explanation: Presentation does not change the physics.

options.text: lagging the beaker and keeping the heater fully submerged
options.explanation: Both cut the energy that leaves the sample unaccounted.

options.text: reading the thermometer from directly above
options.explanation: That reduces parallax, a random error, not leakage.

questions.stem: Which pair lists one random and one systematic error of this practical?

options.text: heat loss (random) and parallax (systematic)
options.explanation: Both are swapped.

options.text: parallax and parallax
options.explanation: One error cannot be both classes.

options.text: neither error exists in this practical
options.explanation: Both classes are present in any heating run.

options.text: parallax on the thermometer (random) and heat loss through the beaker (systematic)
options.explanation: Scatter versus repeatable bias — correctly classified.

questions.stem: State the relation between the graph's gradient and the specific heat capacity.
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient = ΔT ÷ ΔQ = 1 ÷ (m × c), so the specific heat capacity equals 1 divided by the product of mass and gradient.

questions.stem: State two safety precautions specific to using an electric immersion heater with water.
questions.modelAnswer: Keep hands dry and use insulated leads when connecting the mains-powered heater, and protect against scalding hot water with eye protection and safe handling.

questions.stem: Explain why the first few points of the graph often sit closest to the ideal straight line, and why repeating the run with a fresh cool sample tightens the result.
questions.modelAnswer: Early in the run the sample is near room temperature, so the surroundings gap — and therefore the leaked power — is smallest and almost all the metered energy warms the water. Repetition with a fresh cool sample keeps that gap small again and averages the random scatter of thermometer and stopwatch readings, pulling the fitted gradient towards the ideal proportional line.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg sample's ΔT–ΔQ line has a gradient of 0.0016 °C/J over its linear region. Calculate the specific heat capacity.
